newsitem.title: MEXICO: Race starts in earnest for Mexico City mayor's job.
newsitem.headline: Race starts in earnest for Mexico City mayor's job.

text.p: The race for the hotly contested job of mayor of Mexico City kicked off in earnest on Saturday after former left-wing presidential candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas threw his hat into the ring for the July election.
Cardenas joins Mexico City attorney-general Jose Antonio Gonzalez Fernandez as two of the most prominent names to register as their party's candidates for the mayor's job.

Previously the mayor of the huge metropolis was hand picked by the president of the republic, but under changes enacted by President Ernesto Zedillo to foster greater democracy the mayor will instead be elected.
The job carries great political significance in the highly centralized nation.

Mexico City newspaper Reforma carried a banner headline on Saturday saying two-time presidential candidate, Cardenas, would compete against ex-party leader Porfirio Munoz Ledo to represent the Democratic Revolution (PRD) in the mayoral race. The party will chose its official candidate at a convention on March 9.
Up to now, the sprawling, often chaotic capital city has been run by a member of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

Three candidates put forward their names on Friday to continue that tradition and represent the PRI: the president of the legislature in the federal district, Manuel Jimenez Guzman, the former governor of Mexico state, Alfredo del Mazo, and Mexico City's chief prosecutor, Gonzalez Fernandez.
Gonzalez Fernandez has been tipped as Zedillo's favorite, and that will carry much weight during the party's selection convention on Feb. 19.
But whoever wins the chance to represent the PRI will face a rough ride.
Almost all recent opinion polls show the PRI in second or third place in the capital behind the conservative National Action Party (PAN), the number two political force nationwide.
Pollsters say that Mexicans are fed up with rising violent crime, pollution and official corruption, and will be unlikely to give the PRI another chance.
The PAN has two candidates vying for its nomination, with former party president Carlos Castillo Peraza the front runner. The party will select its candidate at its March 2 convention.
